items.title: Gender and LGBTQ+ representation across college majors and achievement levels using nationally representative US data
items.author: Taek H. Kim
items.content: Cimpian et al. demonstrate disparities in representation by gender and LGBTQ+ identity across US college majors and levels of academic achievement. They identify an in-group advantage among lower-achieving students.

items.title: Mourning the loss of AI companions
items.author: Zeliha Oğuz-Uğuralp
items.content: People can form emotional bonds with AI companions. Using two AI product updates as natural experiments and combining with survey evidence, De Freitas et al. show that changes to AI companions can elicit attachment-related loss and restoration desires.

items.title: How contemporary academic structures constrain scientific creativity and hold back early-career researchers
items.author: Teun Everts
items.content: In this Perspective, Haubrock et al. argue that today’s scientific structures constrain creativity and that strategic conformity is a rational response. They discuss how this holds back early-career researchers from reaching their full potential as scientists.

items.title: The gender gap reconsidered
items.author: Bryce E. Hughes
items.content: Gender polarization in fields such as engineering or nursing has served as a barrier to students whose genders do not conform to these norms. Cimpian et al. demonstrate that this polarization also protects lower-performing students who do conform, while impeding LGBTQ+ students in male-dominated fields.

items.title: Saturation of moral language predicts lower content engagement on social media
items.author: Brian Uzzi
items.content: Across more than 1.6 million posts on Twitter, Reddit and 8chan, Candia et al. find that moral language is associated with higher engagement up to a measurable sweet spot. Beyond it, moral saturation is linked to lower engagement.

items.title: Turning biometrics into a commodity raises privacy and governance risks
items.author: Aldo Díaz
items.content: Paying people for their biometrics raises complex ethical and legal questions about consent, privacy and the long-term risks of handing over irrevocable personal data. This Comment examines why such models require caution and what safeguards could better protect the public.
